title: Newman on development
hookLine: doctrine grows like a seed, staying itself while changing

lines: A BABY PHOTO ON THE FRIDGE.
cards: A baby photo stuck to a fridge. Everything about that child has changed since: the height, the voice, the things that make them laugh. Yet nobody at the kitchen table doubts it's the same person.
John Henry Newman, an English priest and writer, needed that puzzle for a bigger question.

Christian teaching seemed to have changed down the centuries: new words, new feasts, new definitions the apostles never wrote down. Had the church drifted away from where it started? Or had it grown up?
Newman wrote a long essay to find out.

teach.b: His answer came from the garden. A true idea, he said, is alive. It grows the way a seed grows into a tree, unfolding what was in it from the start.
An oak doesn't look like an acorn, but it's the same living thing, and nothing in the oak contradicts the seed.
Jesus used this kind of picture: the kingdom of heaven is "like to a grain of mustard seed," sown small, grown into a tree where the birds come and lodge in its branches.
Paul too: "I have planted, Apollos watered; but God gave the increase."
Newman also wrote a sentence people still quote, and today's line comes from it: "In a higher world it is otherwise, but here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often."
He isn't praising every change. Much of his essay asks how to tell true growth from corruption.

teach.h: ACORN TO OAK: THE SAME LIFE
teach.b: Does the new thing keep the same type, the same shape of life?
Does it carry the earlier teaching forward, or quietly cancel it? A tumor grows too.
Newman wrote this while moving from the Church of England into the Catholic Church, so the question was his own. Christians still weigh his answer differently.
Catholic theologians have drawn on him to explain how teaching unfolds over time; Orthodox and Protestant Christians ask their own hard questions about which developments truly grew from the seed.
His puzzle reaches past any one church: how does something living change and stay itself?

how: Catholic teaching often speaks of doctrine developing over time while staying faithful to the apostles, and Newman is studied in that light; other churches discuss the same question in their own ways, through scripture, councils and tradition.

games.why: Newman asked whether a change keeps the same type, the same life, and carries earlier teaching forward. growth, yes; corruption, no.

practice: Bring to mind something that grew and stayed itself: a friendship that's lasted, a tree you've walked past for years, a family recipe tweaked but still tasting like home.
Look for the thread that runs all the way through, then, if you like, turn the question gently on yourself. If you pray, you can give thanks for whatever has grown.

wordCard.voice: Newman on development. John Henry Newman's idea that true teaching grows like a seed: changing shape, keeping the same life.

orig.note: Greek: to make grow — the verb behind 1 Corinthians 3:6, "God gave the increase."

carryVoice: Your line: to live is to change. A new shape, the same life. Until tomorrow.
